AVALON CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  TUESDAY, MARCH 18, 2025 5:00 PM  —

  410 AVALON CANYON ROAD
  AGENDA
In compliance with the Americans with Disability Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting,
please contact the City Clerk’s Office (310) 510-0220. Notification 48 hours prior to the meeting will enable the City
to make reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting. (28 CFR 35. 102-35.104 ADA Title II). All
public records relating to an agenda item on this agenda are available for the public inspection at the time the records
are distributed to all, or a majority of all, members of the City Council. Such records shall be available at City Hall
located at 410 Avalon Canyon Rd.

 For the public’s convenience, but not participation, the meeting can be viewed:
  On local cable: Catalina Broadband Solutions channel 3
  Streaming on Facebook Live: www.facebook.com/CityOfAvalonOfficial
  Streaming on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/CityofAvalonCA

DEPARTMENT HEAD REPORTS

CITY MANAGER REPORT I CITY ATTORNEY REPORT

COUNCILMEMBER REPORTSIREQUESTS I MAYOR REPORT

ORAL COMMUNICATION
Members of the public may address the City Council at this time. No action will be taken on non-
agenda items at this meeting. Speakers should limit comments to two (2) minutes each.

PUBLIC HEARING

1.  TDA Article 8 Hearing
  The Metropolitan Transit Authority (MTA) is required to hold a public hearing on the
  community’s unmet public transit needs in accordance with the Transportation
  Development Act (TDA) Article 8. TDA Article 8 funds are currently being used by the City
  of Avalon to fund Avalon’s Consolidated Land Transportation Program which includes
  DAR and fixed routes.
  Recommended Action
  Open the Public Hearing and accept comments from the public. Close the Public Hearing.

CONSENT CALENDAR

2.  City Council Minutes
  Although the live recording is the official record of public meetings, minutes are prepared
  for the Council’s approval.
  Recommended Action
  Approve minutes from the February 18, 2025 regular City Council Meetings.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
MARCH 18, 2025
PAGE 2

3.  Warrants
  Expenditures Submitted for Approval:
  • US Bank General Account Warrants totaling $1,864,208.40.
  • One payroll totaling $254,084.93.
  • Four electronic fund transfers totaling $156,626.86.
  Recommended Action
  Approve the total expenditures for February 24, 2025 through March 7, 2025 totaling
  $2,274,920.19.

4.  Revisions to the City’s Records Retention Schedules
  Avalon has adopted several records retention schedules over the years. Updates are
  necessary to reduce current and future records storage costs, eliminate duplication of
  effort, increase efficiency and take advantage of current technology and changes in law.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution rescinding Resolution No. 17-37 and adopting a records retention
  schedule authorizing destruction of certain city records.

5.  Fourth of July Fireworks Procurement
  Annually, the City of Avalon provides a fireworks show as a part of the Fourth of July
  Celebration. City Staff solicited quotes from various fireworks and barge vendors and
  received one proposal from each vendor type.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to execute agreements with Garden State Fireworks, Inc. to
  provide the firework show, and Curtin Maritime for the barge services for the Annual
  Fourth of July Celebration.

6.  Edison International Contribution Agreement
  The City of Avalon Fire Chief was contacted by a representative from Edison International
  interested in supporting the City Fire Department with wildland fire efforts. After a number
  of meetings, Edison International agreed to fund the purchase a new fire engine.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager or his designee to execute a Contribution Agreement with
  Edison International.

GENERAL BUSINESS

7.  Catalina Electric Car Company Autoette Rental Permit Application
  On February 11, 2025 the City received a transportation permit application from Mike King
  and Matt Affolder on behalf of Catalina Electric Car Company. The business is requesting
  (12) new electric commercial rental autoette permits with a proposed business facility
  located at Catalina Yamaha at 117 Clarissa Avenue.
  Recommended Action
  Discuss and provide direction to Staff. If consensus for approval is reached, make the
  affirmative findings that the criteria set forth in Avalon Municipal Code Section 5-1 1 have
  been met and direct Staff to issue the appropriate permit.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
MARCH 18, 2025
PAGE 3

8.  Advance Payment of Measure C Funds to the Catalina Island Medical Center (CIMC)
  The Catalina Island Medical Center (CIMC) has asked the City Council to approve
  execution of a non-binding letter of interest ([01) for a potential advance payment of
  approximately $2,8000,000 from the City’s general fund so that CIMC can participate in
  a program to receive a substantial increase in funding.
  Recommended Action
  Provide direction on whether to enter into the letter of interest which could lead to an
  agreement wherein the City advances approximately $2,800,000 for CIMC’s participation
  in the Voluntary Rate Range Intergovernmental Transfer Program, which CIMC believes
  will result in increased funding for CIMC. The City would be paid back through any
  available CIMC revenues, including Measure C funds, over the course of several years.

9.  Options for City Council in Considering Tenant Protection and Rent Control Measures
  The purpose of this item is to provide the City Council with information on State law as it
  relates to tenant protections and rent control, and provide examples of what other cities
  have codified locally so the City Council may consider what policy options it is interested
  in exploring for Avalon.
  Recommended Action
  Consider and discuss tenant protections and rent control options available under State
  law, and provide direction to City of Avalon (“City”) staff to evaluate and report back on
  any desired local options available to the City.

10.  Discussion Regarding Cross Channel Wharfage
  On December 4, 2018 the City Council amended the Avalon Municipal Code increasing
  wharfage by $1.00 roundtrip ($50 each way) and dedicated 100% of the increase to
  further fund capital improvements in the harbor, as planned grant-funded projects
  required local matching funds exceeding existing available revenues. The ordinance took
  effect on March 1, 2019 and was originally scheduled to sunset on February 28, 2021.
  On October 20, 2020, the City Council extended the increase to sunset on June 30, 2025.
  Recommended Action
  Discuss an increase in cross channel wharfage to fund anticipated capital improvements
  in the Harbor.

ADJOURN

posted on Friday, March 14, 2025 on the City’s website, www.cityofavalon.com/agendacenter,
and at City Hall, 410 Avalon Canyon Road.

PUBLIC HEARING

5.  Fiscal Year 2024-2025 Miscellaneous Fee Schedule Revisions
  1. City Council heard a presentation regarding the Miscellaneous Fee Schedule.
  2. Mayor Marshall opened the Public Hearing, no comments were heard. 3.
  Mayor Marshall closed the Public Hearing. 4. City Council adopted Resolution
  No. 25-07 of the City Council of the City of Avalon Setting Fees for Services,
  Facilities and Activities of the City of Avalon for Fiscal Year 2024-25.
  Motion to approve made by Lisa Lavelle, seconded by Michael Ponce. (All Ayes)

GENERAL BUSINESS

6.  Presentation and Discussion on Revisions to Avalon Municipal Code § 4-4
  Vehicles
  City Council heard a presentation to consider updates to the Avalon Municipal
  Code § 4-4 Vehicles and provided direction on the following:
  1) Require permits for motorcycles/motorized scooters. Staff will gather
  information for a future discussion on placing limits on how many motorcycles
  and scooters can be registered per dwelling unit.
  2) Staff will gather information for a future discussion on the possible size
  increase to the Micro-Car Length (120.1” to 135”) & Oversize (200” to 210”).
  3) Allow ADUs/JADUs to qualify for one Residential Autoette Permit per unit with
  off-street parking requirement.
  4) Consider setting caps by permit type at a later date.
  5) Banking of Vehicle Permits-Allow existing blue sticker holder to bank blue
  sticker(s) for a maximum of three years. If blue sticker holder is not able to
  purchase a vehicle within the three years he/she will need to apply for a
  hardship exemption. Moving forward new blue sticker holders will not be
  allowed to bank vehicle permits and will only be allowed to be placed on full
  size vehicles, not on autoettes.
  6) Allow Legacy Permits to continue (as long as renewed on-time).
  7) Allow transfers of blue stickers to a spouse, child, or grandchild prior to death
  as long as they are full-time residents. The City Attorney will gather
  information on the legalities of intergenerational transfers.
  8) Align overnight off-street parking to 2:00 a.m.- 6:00 am.
  9) Electric Commercial Autoette Replacement Program-Applicants can utilize
  existing gas powered autoettes, commercial auotettes that are brought from
  the mainland are required to be electric.
  10) Allow Residential Parking Program to move forward by neighborhood
  application. The program will require a petition (75%+), payment for sign
  installment, and require City Council or Planning Commission approval.

SUBJECT:  Revisions to the City’s Records Retention Schedules

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt a resolution rescinding Resolution No. 17-37 and
adopting a records retention schedule authorizing destruction of certain city records.

REPORT SUMMARY: Avalon has adopted several records retention schedules over the
years. The City Council last adopted records retention schedules on December 19, 2017 by
Resolution No. 17-37.

The City selected Gladwell Governmental Services, Inc., an expert in local government
records, to update its records retention schedules. Updates are necessary to reduce current
and future records storage costs, eliminate duplication of effort, increase efficiency and take
advantage of current technology and changes in law. Resolution No. 17-37 provided City Staff
the ability to make minor modifications to the retention policy without seeking approval from the
City Council; however, the proposed updates do not qualify as minor in nature.

The update to the records retention schedules are driven by many factors, including:
  • Very limited space in City facilities.
  o Many Departments reported they are out of space to store their records.
  • Many departments are filing and storing copies of the same records.
  • Avalon produces and manages many permanent records.
  • Escalating records storage expenses.
  • Technology advancements.
  • Changes in law.

The purpose of the program is to apply efficient and economical methods to the creation,
utilization, maintenance, retention, preservation and disposal of all records managed by the
City.

The retention periods are in compliance with all laws and are standard business practice for
California cities.

It is standard business practice for California cities to authorize the routine destruction of
records that have exceeded their adopted retention period, upon the request of the
 Department Head and with the consent in writing of the City Clerk and City Attorney, which is
provided in Section 2 of the resolution.

It is also standard business practice for California cities to authorize updates to the schedule
without further action of the City Council. The changes, with the written approval signatures,
are retained permanently by the City Clerk and are accessible to the public, and this process
saves substantial taxpayer money.

This period, the following changes are being made:

ALL Schedules:
  • nsDestroy Paper after Imaged & QC’d?” was changed to “Yes: After QC & OD” for
  most records series.
  • The legal requirements for the electronic record to serve as the Official I Original record
  are summarized in the Records Retention Legend in the explanation of the “Destroy
  Paper after Imaged & QC’d” column, as they have been in the past.

City-Wide:

   RESOLUTION NO.

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF
  AVALON, CALIFORNIA, ADOPTING A RECORDS RETENTION
  SCHEDULE, AUTHORIZING DESTRUCTION OF CERTAIN CITY RECORDS, AND
  RESCINDING PREVIOUS RESOLUTION NO. 17-37

  WHEREAS, the maintenance of numerous records is expensive, slows document
retrieval, and is not necessary after a certain period of time for the effective and efficient
operation of the government of the City of Avalon; and

  WHEREAS, Section 34090 of the Government Code of the State of California
provides a procedure whereby any City record which has served its purpose and is no longer
required may be destroyed; and

  WHEREAS, the State of California has adopted guidelines for retention period for
various government records; and

  WHEREAS, the City Council of the City of Avalon adopted Resolutions No. 17-37
adopting a records retention schedule;

  NOW, THEREFORE, THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF AVALON DOES
RESOLVE AS FOLLOWS:

  Section 1. Resolution Number 17-37 is hereby rescinded.

  Section 2. The records of the City of Avalon, as set forth in the Records Retention
Schedule Exhibit A, attached hereto and incorporated herein by this reference, are hereby
authorized to be destroyed as provided by Section 34090 et seq. of the Government Code of
the State of California and in accordance with the provision of said schedule upon the
request of the Department Head and with the consent in writing of the City Clerk and City
Attorney, without further action by the City Council of the City of Avalon.

  Section 3. With the written consent of the City Clerk, City Manager, and City
Attorney, updates are hereby authorized to be made to the Records Retention Schedule
without further action by the City Council.

  Section 4. The term “records” as used herein shall include documents, instructions,
books, microforms, electronic files, magnetic tape, optical media, or papers; as defined by
the California Public Records Act.

  Section 5. The City Clerk shall certify to the passage and adoption of this resolution
 and enter it into the book of original resolutions.

  Section 6. This resolution shall become effective immediately upon its passage and
adoption.

A legend explaining the information presented in the retention schedule; please read this for an explanation
of every column.

The specified retention period applies regardless of the media of the record: If a record is stored on paper
and electronic format (a computer file on a hard drive), all electronic and paper records should be
destroyed (or deleted I erased) after the specified period of time has elapsed and authorization to
destroy has been obtained.

Copies or duplicates of records should never be retained longer than the prescribed period for the official
(original) record, and drafts and copies should be destroyed as soon as they are no longer required.

The term “records” shall include all records as defined by the California Public Records Act.

STRUCTURE: CITY-WIDE. DEPARTMENTS & DIVISIONS

The City-wide retention schedule includes those records all departments have in common (e-mails, letters,
memorandums, purchase orders, etc.). These records are NOT repeated in the Department retention
schedule, unless that department is the Office of Record.

Each department has a separate retention schedule that describes the records that are unique to their
department, or for which they are the Office of Record. The department retention schedules may be
organized by Division within that Department. If a record is not listed in your department retention schedule,
refer to the City-wide retention schedule, or look in the index to the schedules (provided after approval.)

BENEFITS

This retention schedule has been developed by Diane R. Gladwell, MMC, an expert in Municipal
Government records, and will provide the City with the following benefits:

  • Reduce administrative expenses, expedite procedures
  • Free office space and computer storage space
  • Reduce the cost of records storage paper and electronic
  —

  • Eliminate duplication of effort within the City
  • Find records faster
  • Determine what media should be used to store records

AUTHORIZATION TO DESTROY RECORDS (Paoer or Electronic Records’:

Destruction or deletion of an official (original) record that has exceeded its retention period must be
authorized prior to destruction or deletion.

  •  If there is a minimum retention (“Minimum 2 years”), the destruction / deletion must be
  authorized before it is destroyed, as it is an official (original) record.

Copies, drafts, notes and non-records do NOT require authorization, and can be destroyed “When No
Longer Required.”

  •  If there is NOT a minimum retention (“When No Longer Required”), it does NOT need to be
  authorized prior to destruction, as it is a preliminary draft, copy, or the Content is NOT
  Substantive.

On every page of the schedules (near the top, just under the column headings) are important instructions,
including instructions regarding holds on destroying records. “Litigation, complaints, claims, public
records act requests, audits andlor investigations suspend normal retention periods (retention
resumes after settlement or resolution).”

OFR (Office of Record): The department that keeps the Official (original or “record copy”) record for its retention period, then authorizes destruction.
Usually, it is the department that originates the record. The official (original) record may be the paper! hard copy version of the record; however the electronic
record may be the official (original) record. See the “Destroy Paper after Imaged & QC’d” below for the Legal Requirements for the electronic record to be the
official (original) record.

Records Description: The record series (a group of like records).

Non-Record: Documents. studies, books and pamphlets produced by outside agencies, preliminary drafts not retained in the ordinary course of business.

Retention/Disposition:  Active (guideline): How long the file remains in the immediate office area
  Inactive (guideline): How long the file is in off-site storage, stored electronically in accordance with law (see below)
  Total Retention: The total number of years the record is retained

  For file folders containing documents with different retention timeframes, use the document with the longest retention time.
  P = Permanent
  Indefinite No fixed or specified retention period; used for databases, because the data fields are interrelated.

  Vital? = Those records that are needed for basic operations in the event of a disaster.

  Media Options (guideline) terms used in State law:  Mag = Electronic Computer Magnetic Media (Hard drives, Networks, USB Drives, Cloud, etc.)
  Mfr = Microforms (aperture cards, microfilm, microfiche, or jackets)
  Ppr = Paper
  OD = Optical Disk or other Unalterable Media which does not allow changes

  Scan I Import (guideline):  “S’ indicates the record should be scanned into the document imaging system;
  “II” indicates the record should be electronically imported into the document imaging system;
  “M” indicates the record was microfilmed

SUBJECT:  Fourth of July Fireworks Procurement

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager to execute agreements with
Garden State Fireworks, Inc. to provide the firework show, and Curtin Maritime for the barge
services for the Annual Fourth of July Celebration.

REPORT SUMMARY: Annually, the City of Avalon provides a fireworks show as a part of the
Fourth of July Celebration.

City Staff solicited quotes from various fireworks and barge vendors and received one proposal
from each vendor type:
  Fireworks Vendor  Garden State Fireworks, Inc.  $45,300.00
  Barge Vendor  Curtin Maritime  $38,500.00

Garden State Firework Inc. is a licensed fireworks operator and proposes to shoot 2,310 shells
ranging from 1-6” plus 6,500 assorted effects, equaling 8,810 items shot in the air during an
18-minute show. Garden State Firework, Inc. is one of the oldest fireworks companies in the
United States with approximately 143 years in operation. Golden State Fireworks, Inc. has
been the City of Avalon vendor the last three Fourth of July celebrations.

As per a longstanding agreement, Love Catalina pays for the firework show and has
traditionally agreed to fund the show the City Council selects.

The fireworks will be shot off a barge at the mouth of Avalon Harbor. Curtin Maritime has
agreed to provide barge services for the show for their hard costs only (labor and fuel). Any
additional revenue received from the City in excess of hard costs will be donate to youth
organizations on the Island. In 2024, Curtin Maritime donated approximately $30,000 to
Avalon youth programs.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Enhance Recreational Opportunities.

FISCAL IMPACTS: City contributes costs associated with the barge $38,500 and Love
Catalina will pay for the fireworks.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: No fireworks and/or
barge vendor will be selected and the City will not have a fireworks show on July 4, 2025.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Contract barge and firework services.

SUBJECT:  Catalina Electric Car Company Autoette Rental Permit Application

RECOMMENDED ACTION: Discuss and provide direction to Staff. If consensus for approval
is reached, make the affirmative findings that the criteria set forth in Avalon Municipal Code
Section 5-1 1 have been met and direct Staff to issue the appropriate permit.

REPORT SUMMARY: On February 11, 2025 the City received a transportation permit from Mike
King and Matt Affolder on behalf of Catalina Electric Car Company. The business is requesting
(12) new electric commercial rental autoette permits with a proposed business facility located at
Catalina Yamaha at 117 Clarissa Avenue.

The applicant proposes to utilize the Catalina Yamaha facility on Clarissa as well as an area to
provide service and long-term vehicle rentals. Vehicle rentals would be available for periods of
half and full days only. Vehicles would be permitted to be rented overnight for those with off-
street parking or handicap status.

The proposed rentals will meet the established maximum length for Low-Speed

  For over 40 years, Catalina Yamaha has been a vital part of Avalon, offering essential services
like repairs, towing, and tire disposal. California’s shift to electric vehicles has brought new challenges,
resulthg in a significant revenue decline. Without a sustainable income source, we may be forced to
raise service rates substantially or shut down. To preserve these critical services and support Avalon’s
enviromnental goals, we propose launching an all-electric rental fleet to meet the evolving needs of
residents, visitors, and local businesses while advancing sustainability.

Business Challenges
Dedinrng Revenue:
  • New cart sales have declined by 50% since the implementation of electric-only laws.
  • Service revenue has already declined 30% and is projected to drop by 60% as electric
  carts require less maintenance.
  • Over 75% of our gross revenue comes from service and new sales.
Rising Costs:
  • The costs of labor, insurance, and overall business operations are increasing.
  • The average mechanic labor rate in California is $175/hour, but we’ve kept ours at

Service Gaps

  residents and visitors without reliable transportation for longer trips, evening plans, or
  full-day needs.
  • There are no rental services for individuals with mobility challenges, limiting access to
  Avalon’s attractions and reducing inclusivity.
  • No utility vehicle rentals are available for companies leaving construction, production,
  and service needs unmet and creating logistical challenges to working in Avalon.

Proposed Solution
All-Electric Rental Fleet:
  • Operate a 12 electric cart fleet offering full-day rentals (8:00 AM to 5:00 PM) to meet
  Avalon’s need for flexible transportation options.
  • Provide overnight rentals for those with off-street parking or handicap status, supporting
  extended stays and mobifity needs.
  • Offer utility vehicle rentals for construction crews, production teams, and service
  professionals to meet specialized business demands.
 Addressing Market Gaps
Full-Day and Overnight flansportation for Residents and Visitors:

  • Overnight rentals offer dependable solutions for residents dealing with vehicle
  breakdowns, moving, or large projects, ensuring options for any need.
  • Full-day rentals offer visitors flexible options for extended stays or evening plans,
  addressing a critical void in Avalon’s transportation offerings.
Equitable and Inclusive Rental Options for Disabled Individuals:
  • Handicap-accessible carts offered for full-day and overnight rentals provide reliable and
  inclusive transportation, ensuring accessibility and freedom for individuals with mobility
  challenges.
  • These rentals offer dignified, and equitable transportation for disabled visitors and their
  families. This ensures full access to Avalon ‘s attractions while promoting inclusion and
  addressing an essential but unmet need in the market.
Flexible Utility Vehicle Rentals for Business Needs:
  • Utility vehicle rentals for full-day use cater to production crews, construction teams, and
  service professionals, providing reliable transportation for on-site work in Avalon.
  • These rentals cater to the needs of business guests, executives, and contractors,

 Why Choose Catalina Yamaha?

businesses.

offers. Our fleet addresses peak demand when visitors face up to 2-hour wait times for hourly rentals,
providing a more seamless experience through online booking and flexible options. Additionally, we
offer unique rental options like utility vehicles and handicap-accessible carts, filling critical service
gaps in Avalon’s current market and enhancing accessibility for residents, visitors, and businesses alike.

2. Objection: 12 carts is too many. Why not start with a smaller fleet?
  Operating a 12-cart fleet ensures operational efficiency by spreading fixed costs for charging,
maintenance, and insurance across a larger number of units, reducing the cost per cart. This fleet size
addresses key market gaps, including full-day rentals, overnight rentals, and utility vehicle rentals for
production crews, construction projects, and business needs. It also provides the flexibility to meet
peak season demand, preventing service denials during high-traffic periods. A smaller fleet would
result in unmet visitor and resident needs, while a larger fleet increases revenue potential, helping
sustain essential community services like affordable repairs, towing, and tire disposal.

3. Objection: The initiative will overwhelm Avalon’s parking infrastructure.
  Catalina Yamaha has a clear parking plan to ensure minimal impact on Avalon’s public
infrastructure. All carts wifi be stored on private property or at a dedicated charging station near
downtown, preventing the use of public roads or city-owned parking spaces. Overnight rentals are only
available to visitors or residents with proof of off-street parking, further ensuring that public parking
remains unaffected. This approach eliminates reliance on city infrastructure for storage or operational
needs.
  4. Objection: There are afready too many carts on Avalon’s roads.
  Unlike hourly rentals that require multiple daily pick-ups and drop-offs, Catalina Yamaha’s carts
are rented for full-day and overnight use, significantly reducing the number of daily trips on Avalon’s
roads, All carts will be stored on private property or at our designated charging station, ensuring they
do not occupy public roads or city-owned parking spaces. Our fleet also includes electhc utility
vehicles, handicap-accessible carts, and loaner carts for residents, reducing reliance on larger, less
efficient vehicles. This approach supports Avalon’s goal of maintaining clear, uncongested streets while
offering essential transportation services for residents, visitors, and local businesses.

5. Objection: This initiative doesn’t support Avalon’s long-term sustainabiity
goals.
  This initiative directly supports Avalon’s sustainability goals by replacing gas-powered carts
with 100% electric vehicles. Our fleet achieves a 100% reduction in emissions and a 95% reduction in
noise pollution, improving the island’s air quality and enhancing the visitor experience. The charging
station infrastructure provides sustainable LV support for fleet operations and offers the potential to aid
Avalon’s broader transition to electric vehicles. Additionally, we will offer retired rental carts at
affordable prices to Avalon residents, promoting local LV adoption and reducing reliance on gas-
powered carts. This initiative positions Avalon as a leader in eco-friendly tourism and clean
transportation.

6. Objection: Residents don’t need access to rental carts.
  Residents face limited options when their carts break down or require repairs. By offering day
and overnight rental carts Catalina Yamaha ensures that local families and individuals have access to
reliable transportation during their critical times. Residents currently have no access to full-clay or
overnight rental options, and our program directly addresses this gap by providing convenient and
affordable rentals. Additionally, residents can rent utility vehicles for moving, family visits, or large
home projects—services that hourly rental companies do not offer. Our program supports Avalon’s
community members by providing essential transportation solutions not currently available on the
island.

7. Objection: The city will lose control over charging infrastructure and public
space.
  Catalina Yamaha’s charging station will be entirely self-funded and installed on private property
with designated parking spaces, not public right-of-way. The city will not be asked for funds, nor will
public space be utilized for the station’s construction or operations. Our charging infrastructure is
designed to support our fleet operations exclusively, and we will maintain and manage it at no cost to
the city. This charging station also aligns with Avalon’s sustainability goals by supporting electric
vehicle adoption and providing a model for how future EV infrastructure can be implemented.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Provide direction on whether to enter into the letter of interest
which could lead to an agreement wherein the City advances approximately $2,800,000 for

REPORT SUMMARY: The Catalina Island Medical Center (CIMC) has asked the City Council
to approve execution of a non-binding letter of interest (LOl) for a potential advance payment
of approximately $2,8000,000 from the City’s general fund so that CIMC can participate in a
program to receive a substantial increase in funding. The advance would be paid back over the
course of several years through any available CIMC revenues, including Measure C funds. An
explanation of the program and structure of the potential arrangement is discussed below.

The Medicaid program (called “Medi-Cal” in California) is jointly funded by the State of
California and the federal government for certain residents of the State. The State’s share of
the funding is a combination of State funds appropriated to the Department of Health Care
Services (“DHCS”), public funds transferred from other public agencies such as cities or
counties (called “Intergovernmental Transfer” or “IGT”), and certain health care-related taxes.
These funds together represent the “non-federal share” of the funding to pay for Medi-Cal
program expenses and are used to draw down matching federal funds.

The amount of federal funds available depends on the “federal matching assistance
percentage” or “FMAP” and varies by state, by specific services and types of Medicaid
beneficiaries, and by whether the expenses were for administrative purposes or for medical
care delivered to patients. Federal Medicaid managed care rules permit DHCS to annually
develop and certify a range of actuarially sound capitation rates that it will pay to each of
contracted Medi-Cal managed care plans, which must be reviewed and approved each year by
the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in order to be eligible for federal matching
funds.

There is a special program that CIMC wants to participate in to obtain increased funding for its
services. Specifically, the Voluntary Rate Range Intergovernmental Transfer Program was
established in 2011-2012 to allow local public “transferring entities” to contribute their own
funds via IGTs to help DHCS to pay capitation rates to Medi-Cal managed care plans at the
upper bound of the rate range and to draw down matching federal funds based on those higher
rates. The plans must use the “rate range increases” (that is, the difference between the lower

SMRH:4928-1 271-0441.1  -1-
 bound and the upper bound of the range) to make increased payments to health care
providers to increase access to services for their Med i-Cal enrollees.

Participation in the program is voluntary for public transferring entities and each Medi-Cal
managed care plan. For each Medicaid managed care plan year (calendar year), DHCS asks
the managed care plans and transferring entities for their interest in participating in the
Program—demonstrated by completing a non-binding Letter of Interest (“LOl”)—and for
information on the uncompensated care costs for the Medi-Cal enrollees in their plan.

CIMC is asking the City of Avalon to use unallocated funds from the City’s General Fund to
support CIMC’s participation in the Voluntary Rate Range Program with L.A. Care. L.A. Care is
one of the three Medi-Cal managed care plans that covers Medi-Cal members in Los Angeles
County. Most of the Medi-Cal patients who receive services at CIMC are enrolled in L.A. Care.
If approved by the City Council, the City would sign and submit the attached non-binding LOI
included as Attachment A and the attestation included as Attachment B to L.A. Care in order to
demonstrate its interest in participating in the program. L.A. Care must submit these
documents on behalf of all transferring entities to DHCS by March 28, 2025.

Any funds CIMC receives through this program must be used by CIMC for services to Medi
Cal members and cannot be used to pay back the City. The City is expected to be paid back
primarily from the use of funds from Measure C, the sales tax that was approved by City voters
for support of hospital services, as well as other available CIMC revenues. Revenue and
Taxation Code sections 7286.25-7286.26 authorize Avalon to impose a special sales tax to be
used “exclusively for the Avalon Municipal Hospital and Clinic.” This authority is broad and
seems to contemplate that the Hospital could use Measure C funds to repay debt incurred for
the benefit of the Avalon Municipal Hospital and Clinic, regardless of the lender. There is
additional analysis underway of the enforceability of an advance payment agreement between
the City and the Hospital in the event that the Hospital ceases to operate. Until such analysis is
complete, staff does not recommend entering into the final agreement to advance the funds. At
this stage, CIMC is just asking that the City signal its interest in participating in the program,
which is non-binding, and any final agreement will be subject to the City Council’s approval at
a future meeting.

CIMC is seeking to participate in the program as it faces an ongoing structural deficit largely
due to uncompensated care costs associated with serving Medi-Cal patients.

If the proposed IGT is approved by DHCS, DHCS will provide an IGT agreement to the City for
execution by about July 31, 2025, which must be executed by about October 31, 2025. If the
City executes the IGT agreement with DHCS, it will be required to transfer funds to the State
by December 31, 2025.

If the City eventually approves the proposed IGT arrangement, it will seek to enter into an
advance payment agreement with the Hospital, which will include the following key terms:

  1.  Advance Amount: Not to exceed $2,755,862.65
  2.  Primary Source of Repayment: Measure C Funds and other available, CIMC revenues
  3.  Term: 48 months
  4.  Annual Administrative Fee: Equal to 5% of Amount Owed, to account for the lost

SUBJECT:  Options for City Council in Considering Tenant Protection and Rent
  Control Measures

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Consider and discuss tenant protections and rent control
options available under State law, and provide direction to City of Avalon (“City”) staff to
evaluate and report back on any desired local options available to the City.

REPORT SUMMARY: The purpose of this staff report is to provide the City Council with
information on State law as it relates to tenant protections and rent control, and provide
examples of what other cities have codified locally so the City Council may consider what
policy options it is interested in exploring for Avalon.

  I.  City of Avalon’s Municipal Code and Existing Tenant Protections
The City currently has no specific provisions in the Avalon Municipal Code (“AMC”) that impose
City-created rent control (also known as “rent stabilization”). Chapter 9-1 1 of the AMC includes
City-specific Affordable Housing requirements. The purpose of Chapter 9-1 1 is meant to
“[ejncourage the availability of dignified, safe, and affordable workforce housing within the City
of Avalon by promoting development of decent living environments and removing unnecessary
barriers to such development.” (AMC 9-11.101(c).) This includes a City inclusionary housing
requirement to construct a percentage of affordable housing as part of any new residential
development. Specifically, for any new residential development creating five or more for-sale or
rental units, developers are required to set aside at least 20% of those units at an affordable
rent or cost (pursuant to State income limits). However, these City requirements are only
applicable to new commercial or residential development, and do not provide tenant protections
or affordability controls for existing housing stock.

  II.  State Law: The Tenant Protection Act of 2019 and Its Subsequent Changes

A.  2019 Framework, the Tenant Protection Act
In 2019, the State Legislature approved and the Governor signed Assembly Bill 1482, the
Tenant Protection Act (the “Act”). The Act set the “floor” with a series of new tenant protection
measures that must be followed by all California landlords. However, cities can go above that
“floor” in setting more protective local controls for its tenants.

The Act broadly prevents landlords from terminating or declining to renew leases with tenants
of at least a year without “just cause,” as defined under California Civil Code section 1946.2.
 “Just cause” is divided into two categories, “no-fault” termination and “at-fault” termination,
which each have their own eligibility criteria and protections for tenants. The information below
is meant to provide a non-exhaustive summary of the provisions under the Act. Importantly,
when a landlord evicts a tenant under no-fault just cause, the landlord must pay relocation
assistance equal to one-month’s rent, regardless of tenant income1. As described in additional
detail below, a number of cities have required more significant relocation benefits than one-
month, and expanded the types of evictions eligible for relocation benefits.

  •  No-Fault Termination: includes but is not limited to, withdrawal of the unit from the
  rental market; or an intent to demolish or “substantially remodel” the residential
  property.
  o The definition of a “substantial remodel” that qualifies as a no-fault termination
  includes:
  when the remodel “cannot be reasonably accomplished in a safe manner”
  with the tenant present, and requires the tenant to vacate for at least 30
  consecutive days, and either:
  • (1) replacement or substantial modification of any structural,
  electrical, plumbing, or mechanical system that requires a permit; or
  • (2) the abatement of hazardous materials.

  •  At-Fault Termination: includes but is not limited to, instances where tenant is in default
  on rent; breach of any material term of the lease (generally after landlord issues a
  written notice to correct); and a nuisance as defined under State law (including unlawful
  possession of weapons and the manufacture, cultivation, or possession for sale of
  controlled substances).

The Act also includes a statewide “floor” of rent control. Specifically, State law limits rent
increases over a 12-month period, with a maximum increase of no more than 5% plus the
percentage change in the Consumer Price Index (“CPI”), or 10% percent, whichever is
lower.

It is important to note there are a series of exemptions from the applicability of the Act written
into State law. The following reflects a non-exhaustive list of housing types that are not subject
to State law tenant protections, which include: affordable housing restricted by deed or subject
to existing rent or price controls; dormitories; single-family, owner-occupied residences;
housing less than 15 years old; and some mobilehomes.

B.  State Law Amendments Strengthening the Act (SB 567)

Senate Bill 567, which became operative on April 1, 2024, tightened the rules for no-fault just
cause evictions, substantial remodels and rent increases. SB 567 created stricter enforcement
rules to reduce the ability of landlords to evict tenants and then rent out the unit at market rate.

1 To be eligible,
  a tenant must have continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months or
more.
   For an eviction by the landlord because the landlord or their family member will be moving into
  a dwelling unit with an existing tenant (a type of no-fault just cause eviction), the landlord or
  family member must not already live on the property or have access to another vacant unit on
  the property. The landlord or family member also must move in within 90 days of the tenant
  moving out, and stay in the unit for at least a year. Tenants have the right to know the
  relationship of any family member who is moving in, and can request proof. A vacating tenant
  is also given the opportunity to move back in at the same rent rate, along with moving
  expenses, if the landlord or family member does not move in within the specified timeframe or
  fails to stay for the full year.

For substantial remodels, landlords must provide a detailed notice outlining the work to be
done, any necessary permits, and inform tenants that they can return to their units if the work
is not completed or if they do not need to vacate during certain days.

Regarding the Act’s rent control provisions, SB 567 introduced penalties for landlords who
collect rent above the maximum allowed, based on the rent amount that was overcharged, that
may also include attorneys’ fees and court costs. A landlord may also be penalized up to three
times the amount of charged rent, if they acted willfully or with malice. They may also be liable
for damages. These new laws did not change the existing law on rent control or
allowable rent increases under the Act.

It is important to note that as a general rule, the State-adopted Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing
Act (“Costa-Hawkins”) limits the extent to which cities and counties can enact rent control or
rent stabilization ordinances. Specifically, the City of Avalon could only adopt a rent control
measure that applied to apartments (excluding single family homes and/or condominiums) that
received their certificate of occupancy before February 1, 1995. Costa Hawkins allows only
the owner/landlord (and not local government) to set the rental rates for units that received
certificates of occupancy after February 1, 19952. Additionally, cities and counties can
legislate only on rental increases, and may not set the initial rental rate. For those reasons,
in all the cities and counties with rent control ordinances that are described below, any time a
tenant voluntarily moves out, the landlord is permitted to set the new rent without restriction,
based on the new tenancy.

On November 5th 2024, California voters rejected Proposition 33, which would have eliminated
Costa-Hawkins and given cities and counties more rent control authority while also preventing
the State from taking future actions that limit local rent control.

C.  New California Laws with Additional Tenant Protections
There are two, additional new laws aimed at improving housing security and protecting tenants
from unfair evictions and rent increases that are described briefly below.

  •  AB 12: Limits the security deposit landlords can collect to a maximum of one
  month’s rent. An exception is made for “small property” owners (those with no
  more than two properties and a total of four or fewer units), who may still collect
  up to two months’ rent.
2  See CaIfornia Civil Code section 1954.52.
   •  AB 1418: Prevents local governments from adopting regulations that encourage
  evicting tenants based on calls to law enforcement, alleged criminal activity, or
  other alleged nuisances. AB 1418 also prohibits local governments from requiring
  or encouraging landlords to conduct criminal background checks when screening
  tenants.

  Ill. Examples of Tenant Protection and Rent Control Actions Taken by Other Cities

The City Council may provide direction to codify requirements set out under State law so
Avalon may take local, administrative enforcement action, including issuing administrative
citations that include City approved penalty amounts, or adding local civil or criminal remedies.
The City Council may also provide direction for City staff to evaluate  for possible future
  —

review and adoption more protective local tenant protection and rent control actions. Below
  —

are examples of what a number of other cities have done, that can serve as a reference point
for what may be of interest to Ava Ion.

A majority of the cities cited below are charter cities. Charter cities have greater authority to
govern themselves than a general law city, like Avalon. However, and as described above, the
Tenant Protection Act and related State laws provide the “floor,” not the ceiling. State law
allows local tenant protection and/or rent control ordinances so long as they provide the same
or better protections for tenants, with corresponding findings that the local ordinance is both
consistent and “more protective” than State law. This is true for both charter cities and general
law cities.

Accordingly, should Council provide direction to evaluate rent control in the City of Avalon, the
City’s ordinance can be more protective than the “floor” set out under the Act, should ensure a
process by which landlords can petition (appeal) the City to increase the otherwise allowable
rent increase for a fair return of investment, and finally, upon direction, our office will ensure
the proposed local ordinance is otherwise consistent and not preempted by any State or
Federal law (including Costa-Hawkins)  . Any adopted ordinance should also evidence the
City’s interest in promoting long-term stability and certainty for renters, in addition to any other
Avalon-specific public purposes.

Whatever direction the City Council provides, City staff will work with the City Attorney’s Office
to ensure any proposed policy change on tenant protections and/or rent control that come back
to the City Council are vetted consistent with State law.

A.  Examples of Locally-adopted Rent ControllRent Stabilization Ordinances

  •  Culver City. Culver City has adopted a series of more expansive rent control and
  tenant protections than under State law. For relocation assistance, Culver City requires
  a relocation fee to be the greater of three times the tenant’s current monthly rent or an
  amount established U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (“HUD”)
  formula that is based on fair market rent.
 Culver City does not allow no-fault just cause eviction when the tenant is 62 years or
older, is disabled or terminally ill, is a qualifying low-income tenant under State income
limits, or when the tenant has school-aged children who are protected from eviction
during the school year term.

Culver City caps annual rent increases at no more than 5% annually. However, if the
percentage change to the consumer price index (“CPI”) on an annual basis is less than
2%, rent increases in Culver City may not exceed 2% that year. If CPI is greater than
5%, the annual 5% cap still applies and no increase may exceed that percentage.
There are exemptions, including but not limited to, when State or Federal law expressly
exempts the unit from price control and when the landlord receives government
subsidies for the unit. Importantly, Culver City’s rent control measures apply only to
otherwise eligible units that received their certificate of occupancy before February 1,
1995. This threshold date is within local rent control measures, since it is controlled
under State law (see discussion above on Costa-Hawkins).

Similar to other cities and regulations discussed in additional detail below, landlords
may petition the city if they believe the rent control regulations prevent them from
earning a fair return on their property investment.

For no-fault terminations, such as property demolition or when a landlord or their
relative is moving in, Culver City requires landlords to pay relocation assistance. This
amount is typically three times the monthly rent plus an additional $1,000. Small
landlords, defined as those owning three or fewer units, are required to pay less.
Landlords can deduct any past due rent from the relocation payment.

Landlords in Culver City must also register their rental units annually with the city, and
pay an annual fee per rental unit. Culver City’s annual fee is established by City
Council resolution, meant to recover the City’s reasonable costs managing the program
(similar to other cities with annual registration fees, described below). A penalty is
imposed for late registration, and Culver City has enforcement mechanisms in place to
ensure compliance. This includes issuing administrative citations with fines of up to
$1,000 per day. Culver City may also bring civil actions against landlords who violate
these regulations.

County of Los Angeles. The County of Los Angeles imposed rent control on units in
unincorporated areas of the county via an ordinance in 2018, and have been expanding
and refining its codified provisions since that time. The County’s Department of
Consumer and Business Affairs (County Department”) is responsible for the calculation
of the annual, allowable rent increase, for evaluating landlord petitions seeking a higher
increase based on a fair return of investment theory, and also runs the County registry.
The County Department promulgates the necessary procedures and guidelines for how
the program is run.
   The County of Los Angeles has rent control limits for qualifying rental units, and
  separately for “luxury units” as defined. A “luxury unit” has 2-bedrooms or less, is
  located in a complex with at least 25 dwelling units, and, as of September 11, 2018,
  charges more than $4,000 per month in rent. Over calendar year 2023, an annual rent
  increase was limited to 5% for luxury units. Currently, the annual rent increase shall not
  exceed 10% for luxury units, though the County Department retains the ability to amend
  that percentage in the future.

  Only one rent increase is allowed over a 12-month period, and any rent paid in excess
  of the local ordinance must be reimbursed to the tenant. Units subject to the county’s
  rent control are required to be within buildings with two or more units, and for the
  reasons discussed above, must have received their Certificate of Occupancy (or
  equivalent) on or before February 1, 1995.

  For all non-luxury units” subject to rent control, the formula is calculated by the County
  Department annually based on the following evaluation of the Consumer Price Index
  (“CPI”) for the Los Angeles-Riverside-Orange County, California area:

  o  1. If the change in CPI is eight percent (8%) or higher, the maximum allowable
  annual rent increase will be eight percent (8%);
  o  2. If the change in CPI is between three percent (3%) and eight percent (8%), the
  maximum allowable annual rent increase will be equal to the change in CPI;
  o  3. If the change in CPI is between one percent (1%) and three percent (3%), the
  maximum allowable annual rent increase will be equal to three percent (3%);
  o  4. If the change in CPI is between negative two percent (-2%) and one percent
  (1%), the maximum allowable annual rent increase will be equal to the change in
  CPI plus two percent (2%); and
  o  5. If the change in CPI is less than negative two percent (-2%), no annual rent
  increase is permitted.

  However, for calendar year 2024, the county’s ordinance limits the maximum
  allowable rent increase permitted to 4%. Additionally, the Board of Supervisors, by a
  3-2 vote this past June, provided additional direction for staff to evaluate a more tenant-
  protective rent cap of 3% for qualifying rental unit, with 4% permitted for smaller
  property owners, and 5% for luxury units3.

  Landlords may file an application with the County Department if they do not believe they
  are receiving a fair and reasonable return on their investment based on the allowable
  rent increase. The Los Angeles County Code includes a rebuttal presumption that the
  rent increase is fair and reasonable, and the landlord has the burden to prove the
  necessity of any additional rent increase to earn a fair and reasonable return. The
  county evaluates a number of factors to determine whether the landlord has proven the
  burden to increase rent above the set formula, including but not limited to: rental history;

•  Santa Ana. Beginning in 2021, Santa Ana limited annual rent increases to no more
  than 3% of the current rent, or 80% of the change in the Consumer Price Index,
  whichever is less. If the change in the CPI is negative, no rent increase is allowed.
  Currently, 3% is the maximum allowable rent increase “for the period of September 1,
  2024 through August 31, 2025,” based on applicable CPI.4 The City announces the
  allowable rent increase amount no later than June 30 of each year. Like other
  jurisdictions described herein, Santa Ana’s rent control provisions do not apply to units
  exempt under Costa-Hawkins (including units that received a certificate of occupancy
  after February 1, 1995).

  Santa Ana included findings within its adopted ordinance that a CPI-based increase
  provides a just and reasonable return on landlord’s property, adopted to: “encourage
  good management, reward efficiency, and discourage the flight of capital, as well as to
  be commensurate with returns on comparable investments, but not so high as to defeat
  the purpose of curtailing excessive Rents and rental increases.”

  Santa Ana does allow a landlord to submit a petition to the Rent Stabilization Program
  Administrator (a role selected by the City Manager), requesting a rent increase in
  excess of what is otherwise allowed. In evaluating a petition, the Program Administrator
  appoints an impartial hearing officer, who looks to many of the same factors utilized in
  other jurisdictions (rental history; changes in property taxes; the need for repairs, etc.).
  In addition, a Santa Ana hearing officer may evaluate changes in utility charges,
  reasonable operating expenses, and compare the rent lawfully charged to comparable
  rental units in the City of Santa Ana in making their determination.

  Landlords may also submit a “Capital Improvement Petition” to the Program
  Administrator seeking a pass-through of certain costs to tenants to construct capital
  improvements in the unit. Such capital improvements include but are not limited to
  structural, electrical, plumbing, or mechanism systems; roofing; carpeting; and air
  conditioning systems. Santa Ana requires that pass-through costs must be calculated
   by looking at the amortization over the useful life of the improvement, but in no instance
  may the cost exceed 10% of the current rent.

  •  Ojai. The City of Ojai’s ordinance limits annual rent increases to 4%, which the City
  finds provides a just and reasonable return on a landlord’s property, and includes the
  same public purpose as Santa Ana (e.g. the rent cap encourage good management,
  rewards efficiency, and discourage the flight of capital). Ojai, like other jurisdictions
  described above, allows landlords to petition the city for an additional increase as
  necessary for their reasonable return on investment. The landlord must provide notice
  to the tenant of their petition, and the landlord is responsible for all costs associated with
  Ojai’s review of that rent adjustment petition. In Ojai, the Community Development
  Director holds a noticed public hearing within 60 days following the submittal of a
  complete petition, and the Director’s decision is ultimately appealable to the Planning
  Commission.

  •  Sacramento. The City of Sacramento follows the Act and applicable State law as it
  relates to rent control: an annual increase can be 5% plus the percentage change in the
  annual cost of living. Similar to other jurisdictions, Sacramento also includes the right of
  a landlord to petition for a higher amount than the annual rent adjustment. In
  Sacramento, the landlord must demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that
  such an adjustment is necessary to provide the landlord a fair rate of return. A hearing
  examiner looks at a series of factors in considering the petition, some of which overlap
  with other jurisdictions, including but not limited to: change in property taxes;
  unavoidable increases or decreases in maintenance and operating expenses; planned
  improvements or deterioration of the unit; and (specific to Sacramento) any change in
  number of tenants and compliance with Sacramento’s Housing Services.

  Sacramento, similar to other jurisdictions, sets the annual tenant protection program
  fee, as established by the city council an annual basis to fund the city’s costs. In
  Sacramento, the City Manager is empowered to adopt administrative procedures to
  implement the rent control obligations.

B.  Examples of Other Tenant Protections, Adopted Locally:

  •  Long Beach. The City of Long Beach offers increased relocation payments for any
  tenants displaced due to City’s code enforcement activities; for instance, when the
  Building Official issues a notice to vacate for necessary repairs of the unit. Finding that
  low income tenants were most at risk of being displaced for substantial repairs,
  remodels or demolition, Long Beach requires relocation benefits in the amount of
  $3,366.00 per household, with additional payments due when the tenant is disabled.
  Additionally, Long Beach imposes a penalty, in an amount not to exceed $10,000, for
  failure to make timely, required relocation payments on a specific property with a
  displaced tenant.

  •  Pasadena. Pasadena includes heightened relocation benefits for tenants that are in
  “good standing” (generally meaning the tenant is not in breach of their rental
   agreement) in households at or below 140% of the median income. In that instance,
  landlords are required to provide two and half months in fair market rents as established
  by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (“HUD”), for a rental unit of
  a similar size. Pasadena also requires landlords pay a $1,306.00 moving expense for
  adult households, or $3,935.00 for households with dependents, disabled, or senior
  members5. There are exceptions from these relocation requirements for single family
  homes and condominium units.

  Pasadena also offers temporary relocation benefits if a landlord is required to
  temporarily (less than 120 days) recover possession of a rental unit. In those instances,
  the tenant should be paid an amount based on a daily rate equal to two (2) times the
  daily pro-rata portion of the rental rate. The landlord must also pay actual costs
  associated with moving and storage.

FISCAL IMPACTS: None.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City will still follow
the requirements of State law, including the Tenant Protection Act, and its existing Municipal
Code requirements, but will not provide direction to explore additional tenant protections.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: That the City Council provide City staff with direction regarding what, if
any, tenant protections and/or rent control measures that are permissible under State law
should be explored for the City of Avalon.

  CITY OF AVALON CITY COUNCIL

MEETING DATE:  March 18, 2025  AGENDA ITEM:  I
ORIGINATING DEP:  Finance  CITY MANAGER:

PREPARED BY:  Matthew Baker, Finance Director

SUBJECT:  Discussion Regarding Cross Channel Wharfage

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Discuss an increase in cross channel wharfage to fund
anticipated capital improvements in the Harbor.

REPORT SUMMARY: Prior to March 2019, the City charged cross-channel passengers $5.00
round-trip ($2.50 each way) for use of the harbor facilities and dedicated 25% of the revenues
collected to fund capital improvements in the harbor, including to be used as required local
matching funds for grant-funded projects. On December 4, 2018 the City Council amended the
Avalon Municipal Code increasing wharfage by $1.00 roundtrip ($50 each way) and dedicated
100% of the increase to further fund capital improvements in the harbor, as planned grant-
funded projects required local matching funds exceeding existing available revenues. The
ordinance took effect on March 1, 2019 and was originally scheduled to sunset on February
28, 2021. On October 20, 2020, the City Council extended the increase to sunset on June 30,
2025.

From inception through December 31, 2024, the increase in the per passenger wharfage rate
has contributed an additional $3.58 million in harbor revenues to fund capital projects. Below is
a summary of projects in excess of $100,000 identified in the initial staff report that have been
funded utilizing the increased wharfage revenues:

Project  Est. Cost  Actual Costs
  (Net of Grants)  (Net of Grants)
Cabrillo Mole Substructure Repairs (Phase 1)  $2,650,000  $2,706,448
Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal (Phase 2)  500,000  524,493
Pump-out Station  280,000  202,429
Emergency Sea Wall Repairs  200,000  195,077
Total  $3,630,000  $3,627,447

Other harbor capital improvements completed since the adoption of the rate increase include
the Fuel Tank Replacement Project ($1.45 million), Float 1-5 Rehabilitations ($568 thousand),
Green Pier Rehabilitation ($463 thousand), patrol fleet improvements ($347 thousand), End
Float Rehabilitation ($225 thousand), Casino Way Arch ($143 thousand), South Beach
Seawall ($141 thousand), and other smaller capital improvements. In addition, wharfage
revenues dedicated to capital fund annual capital maintenance, including the Harbor Master
 Building, Mole terminal, restroom facilities, and other premises, floats, moorings, ramps, and
emergency maintenance activities related to storm damage.

The Harbor Fund is an enterprise fund and the costs associated with harbor operations and
the maintenance of harbor infrastructure should be recouped through various charges on users
of harbor facilities. The cost to operate the harbor increases annually and revenues need to
grow to cover these increased costs. The majority of harbor revenues are collected from
wharfage fees which are charged to cross-channel and cruise ship operators on a per
passenger basis. Unlike other harbor use fees that are assessed as a percentage of the
operator’s gross receipts or are subject to annual increases through the miscellaneous fee
schedule (e.g. nightly mooring rates), wharfage fees have not been scheduled to increase
annually.

City Staff is proposing the City Council does not allow the wharfage rate to sunset, but rather
increase the rate by $2.00 on cross channel carriers departing from Avalon Harbor. The
increase is necessary to fund planned projects in the Harbor anticipated to begin construction
within the next fiscal year. The proposed application of the fee on departures is to balance the
current $2.00 Measure H special tax assessed on arrivals and would result in a total cost
imposed by the City of $10.00 round-trip ($8.00 for Cross Channel Wharfage and $2.00
Measure H Special Tax). This would generate an additional $1 .35 million in new cross-channel
wharfage revenues dedicated to fund capital projects.

The existing cross channel wharfage generates approximately $1.5 million annually in
revenues to fund capital maintenance and improvements in the Harbor. If the existing rate
were to sunset, revenues available for capital improvements would be reduced by
approximately $650 thousand annually. While the current revenues are sufficient to fund the
rehabilitation of floats, harbor fleet upgrades and other facility improvements, the City is
actively pursuing several large capital projects in the Harbor that are not currently fully funded
with the existing harbor revenues.

The Cabrillo Mole is one of the most important City-owned facilities on the Island serving as
the primary point of entry for the Island’s residents and visitors. The City plans to raise the
current structure to build a new modern facility that will include ticketing facilities, additional
parking, covered queuing areas and additional restrooms. The total projected is budgeted at
approximately $20 million with approximately $8 million allocated in the FY 2024-25 CIP Plan,
Project #180005. The City has been awarded approximately $14 million in grant funding for
this project, with $6 million in cross channel wharfage revenues required to provide the local
match.

In addition, the Green Pleasure Pier is in need of significant structural repairs. In 2018, City
Staff developed a long term maintenance plan including repair and replacement of the
structural piles and decking. The City is actively soliciting bids from qualified firms to replace
between 5 to 20 structural piles. The final project scope will be determined by available budget
balanced with demonstrated value to the City relative to the cost of one mobilization/demolition
as more additive packages are awarded. The total projected is budgeted at approximately $2.2
million with $1 million currently allocated in the FY 2024-25 CIP Plan, Project #180049.
 Though the City is currently seeking grant funding for this project, at this time the project is
scheduled to be funded entirely through cross channel wharfage revenues.

Lastly, the City has comprehensive plans to repair structurally significant areas of South
Beach. The intent of the project is to replace the groin wall/wingwall to protect the beach from
propeller/jet wash, restore approximately 80 feet of existing seawall, rehabilitate the access
stairway and boat launch, and replenish approximately 6,000 cubic yards of beach sand. While
the current budget estimates a total project cost of $975,000 with $200,000 allocated in the FY
2024-25 CIP Plan, Project #205004, the City now estimates the project to cost $2 miliion.
Though the City is currently seeking grant funding for this project, at this time the project is
scheduled to be funded entirely through cross channel wharfage revenues.

If approved, City Staff will bring back to City Council a drafted ordinance for their consideration
once the City Attorney has completed review of the matter. Additionally, Staff proposes
revisiting the wharfage rate at a regularly scheduled City Council meeting at least every two
years, or as directed by Council, to demonstrate the value to the public from the increased
wharfage rates.

FISCAL IMPACTS: If approved, the modification to the wharfage fee is projected to increase
the Capital Improvement Funds within the Harbor Fund (account #10425-8530) by $1.35
million annually.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: If the City Council
determines not to extend the wharfage fee, the Harbor will not have sufficient funds to make
critical improvements to its infrastructure.
